blocks.text: Merging intervals only needs the sorted list. But counting *how many* are active at once needs a sharper tool: break each interval into two **events** and sort those instead.
An interval `[2, 7]` becomes two things that happen:

blocks.code:
at time 2:  +1   (something starts)
at time 7:  -1   (something ends)

blocks.text: Throw away the pairing entirely. Now you have a flat list of timestamped changes, and sweeping it while keeping a running total tells you the number of active intervals at every moment.
Look closely at `|| a[1] - b[1]` in the comparator. When two events share a timestamp, the `-1` sorts before the `+1`, because −1 < 1.

That means an interval ending at time 5 is processed before one starting at time 5 — so they are **not** counted as simultaneous. If your problem treats touching intervals as overlapping, flip that tie-break. One character, opposite answers.
The naive approach asks, for every interval, how many others overlap it — O(N²). The sweep touches each event once after sorting, so the running total is maintained for free.
**O(N log N)** for the sort, **O(N)** for the sweep.

items: **Maximum concurrent meetings** — the peak of the running count, which is also the minimum number of rooms required.
**Finding free gaps** — stretches where the count sits at zero.
**Total covered length** — accumulate time while the count is above zero.

blocks.text: The reframing is the valuable part: stop thinking about objects with extent, start thinking about moments when something changes.
